resolved_conflicts.explanation: Our record lists a fourth-order original lens (USLHS). The NHL nomination and LighthouseFriends say the original was third-and-a-half order, replaced by a fourth-order Sautter lens after the 1877 ice damage.
LighthouseFriends dates Barney's letter to 1821; the NHL nomination cites it as 22 December 1823.

notes_for_editor: NHL nomination OCR is garbled in places (distance from the point read as 'VA miles'); location sentence uses LighthouseFriends. Fiscal-year caveat: the 1894 Board report text prints the year as 1804 (OCR); page given as scan 429 only. Several storm and repair facts (1877, 1883, 1886-87, 1918) come second-hand via the NHL nomination citing Light-House Board reports, which are not in the local corpus for those years. The nomination's chronology of the Coast Guard demolition plan ('early 1980s') sits oddly with NRHP listing in 1975 and LighthouseFriends dating the evaluation to 1972; the text says so. LighthouseFriends tells the 1903 Addicks story differently (keeper ashore for groceries); the Evening Capital says White was on vacation, so the text follows the paper. The 1921 Bulletin commendation of keeper J. E. English prints the station as 'Va.' and was left out. The Bulletin's 1916 note says 6 miles to Annapolis; the Evening Capital 1903 gave 10 miles (omitted). NHL designation year 1999 not independently sourced here and not stated in the story; Lighthouse Society tour page headline about a 1970s head keeper (John White) deliberately not linked to roster entry John W. White. Owner City of Annapolis per LighthouseFriends only. Roster names matched from printed USLHS lines, which are not an OCR table by position. Fact-check 2026-10-27: roster (keepers) lists a selection of the 182 USLHS lines, not every one; Kaufman is on the USLHS roster from 1981. Evening Capital 1903: White was ashore when he saw the light (not 'back at the light'); article says light is 10 miles below Annapolis and near the mouth of the West River (not used).
